name: Decorative decals/coatings on tableware
anchor: EU food-contact framework Regulation 1935/2004 with Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II specific migration limits as the only element-migration instrument in the register expressed in the food-contact FOOD basis (the register's other migration instruments — the EU 2009/48 toy Categories I to III and the ASTM F963 soluble limits — are in the toy article-extraction basis and are barred from every row of this category). Rows whose principal food-contact surface is a polymer anchor it directly, or by disclosed read-across where the instrument's own scope article excludes or does not reach the material or where the taxonomy row also carries a non-plastic configuration. Metal, alloy, ceramic-glaze, vitreous-enamel and glass rows, and the two water-treatment-device rows, are controls because their dedicated release regimes (Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by 2005/31/EC, the metals-and-alloys release regime, and the drinking-water device route) are not in the register in their own jurisdictions' rows. Where one taxonomy row carries both a polymer and a metal configuration, the published cells take the metal-article control and the plastics value is disclosed as a film-only companion.
native_basis: element release from the glaze, vitreous enamel or glass into food or food simulant, declared in TWO native bases: ug/dm2 of food-contact surface for non-fillable and shallow articles and for decoration within 20 mm of the lip (Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention), and ug/L of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III), reportable as ug/kg only on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention
native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, declared in TWO NATIVE BASES because the governing release regime is written in two and this row never merges them. BASIS A, for non-fillable and shallow articles and for any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip: ug per dm2 of food-contact surface, the Directive 84/500/EEC Category I convention. BASIS B, for fillable articles (Category II) and for articles over three litres and cooking ware (Category III): ug per litre of 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract, reportable as ug/kg ONLY on the explicitly stated 1 L = 1 kg convention, which is the single unit conversion this row permits. CONVERSION OF A PER-AREA RESULT INTO A PER-MASS OR PER-VOLUME RESULT IS FORBIDDEN on this row: it requires a food-contact-area-per-kg-of-food assumption (the occurrence literature commonly uses 5 dm2 per kg of foodstuff) that this standard does not adopt, and adopting it would smuggle an unstated assumption into a certification number. Every result is reported in the basis its article form generates, and a per-dm2 result and a per-litre result are never pooled, averaged or compared. This is a RELEASE basis and not a total-content basis, and it is deliberately NOT the Reg (EU) 10/2011 plastics-simulant convention: a plastics specific migration limit is never substituted for a release limit on this family.
scope_note: The decoration itself, considered separately from the article it is applied to, because decoration is a distinct release surface with a distinct exposure route. Decoration that lies on an interior surface is a fill-contact pathway. Decoration within 20 mm of the lip is a LIP-CONTACT pathway, and decoration on the exterior body is a HAND-TO-MOUTH pathway; none of the three is represented by a fill extraction on an undecorated area. The applicable lead-and-cadmium release regime for applied decoration on tableware (EU 84/500/EEC and its amendments, the FDA compliance-policy guides on ceramicware and decorated glassware, and the Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments) is not present in the register as rows of its own jurisdiction; the only register rows carrying those numbers for this article class are four non-allowlisted Uruguayan rows, named and declined on stated grounds in every cell. The row is a control and the gap is recorded.
material: On-glaze and in-glaze ceramic enamel decals and transfers; organic overprint and lustre; applied vitreous enamel bands; gold and platinum lustre; painted and powder-coated exterior surfaces on drinkware.
components: Sample and report separately: (1) each decal, enamel and lustre colour as its own lot, since release is colour-specific; (2) decoration on interior surfaces, by fill extraction; (3) decoration within 20 mm of the lip, by the lip-and-rim convention; (4) exterior body decoration, by a hand-contact wipe and extraction; (5) gold and platinum lustre and any metallic band, which additionally carry an alloy-impurity route; (6) decoration after the declared number of dishwasher cycles, because abraded and etched enamel releases more than as-supplied enamel.
basis_guard: element release|specific release|release into food|release into a food simulant|release into the food simulant|acetic acid|food-contact surface area|mg/dm2|per dm2
basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as element RELEASE from a glaze, vitreous-enamel or glass food-contact surface into food, a food simulant or the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid extract convention, per dm2 of food-contact surface or per litre of extract, may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap. DECLARED VACUOUS STATE (recorded, not overlooked): as written this guard matches ZERO live, non-draft and non-quarantined rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and that is its intended state. The release regime this row's basis family belongs to is not in the register in any form this row may bind, which is the same fact this row's control cells record and state in detail; a guard that admitted a live row today could only do so by admitting a foreign basis. The guard is nevertheless expressed in the register's own basis vocabulary (element or specific release, release into food or a food simulant, 4 percent acetic acid extract, per dm2 of food-contact surface, net device contribution to the treated water) so that a future correct ingest of that regime BINDS through it. The previous prose-sentence guard on this row would have REJECTED the very instruments it was waiting for and forced them to a gap, which is the defect this rewrite removes. Two limits on the guard's force are stated plainly rather than left implicit: the compiler returns on the control branch before basis resolution, so a guard is never evaluated on a control cell, and this note rather than the machine is what carries the guard's force on this row today. The engine change that would close that hole - an assertion that every declared basis_guard either matches at least one live register row or carries basis_guard_vacuous_by_design, failing the build otherwise - is recorded as a tooling gap and is outside this config's scope.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only): the strictest applicable sovereign maximum for this exact product form expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant; a disclosed read-across from the nearest applicable sovereign value in the same basis where the food-contact material family is expressly excluded from or not reached by that instrument; a substantiated not-material determination; or a control. No cell is occurrence-derived, and no cell borrows a value across a basis.

Pb.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is available to anchor this cell, and the register position is stated exactly rather than by assertion of absence. The regime that governs this material family in the real world is EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by Directive 2005/31/EC, supported in the United States by the FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware and by the California Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments; none of those instruments is present in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv as a row of its own jurisdiction, and each is recorded as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. What the register DOES hold for this exact article class is named here rather than passed over: four Uruguayan Reglamento Bromatologico Nacional section 12.5.13 rows carrying the same numbers as the EU Category II and Category III release values, namely uy_rbn_pb_ceramic_fillable_objects_4mgkg (lead, 4000 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_ceramic_fillable_objects_0_3mgkg (cadmium, 300 ug/kg), both scoped to food-contact ceramic objects that can be filled, and uy_rbn_pb_cookware_storage_gt3l_1_5mgkg (lead, 1500 ug/kg) and uy_rbn_cd_cookware_storage_gt3l_0_1mgkg (cadmium, 100 ug/kg), both scoped to ceramic cooking utensils, packaging and storage containers with capacity over three litres. Those four rows are DECLINED on three stated grounds, and not because they are absent. First, Uruguay sits OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so it cannot supply a published number without a recorded governance ruling; this is the same treatment already given on the metal rows to Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29, and it is a jurisdictional gate rather than a judgement about Uruguayan law. Second, the register normalises those rows to a per-MASS figure carrying basis_class as_sold, while the regime they transcribe is expressed per volume of 4 percent acetic acid extract for fillable articles and per unit of food-contact surface area for flat and shallow ones, so binding them would publish a number in a basis the register row does not resolve. Third, they reach only the fillable (Category II) and over-three-litre and cooking-ware (Category III) configurations; no register row covers the Category I flat, shallow and lip-band configuration, which on a decorated plate or a drinking-vessel rim is the higher-release configuration and the one a ceiling would most need to govern. This build separately refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory release testing and no invented number until 84/500/EEC as amended is ingested in its own EU rows and native bases. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. This row's unit of test is the decoration colour, not the article: each colour is a separate lot, and the three exposure routes (fill, lip and hand-to-mouth) are reported separately rather than pooled.
Pb.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration. Each result is reported in the native basis its article form generates and in no other: per dm2 of food-contact surface for a non-fillable or shallow article and for the decoration band within 20 mm of the lip, and per litre of extract (reportable as ug/kg on the stated 1 L = 1 kg convention) for a fillable article and for an article over three litres or intended for cooking. A per-dm2 result is never converted to a per-mass or per-volume result, and per-area and per-volume results are never pooled.

MeHg.rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains. A glaze, an enamel and a glass network are fired inorganic matrices with no organic carbon and no methylation pathway, and no credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for any food-contact material. Total mercury remains a mandatory control on this row; methylmercury is not material and never substitutes for it.
MeHg.reference_method: Total-mercury release determination per the tHg control; reflex methylmercury speciation only where total mercury is detected in the acid extract.
MeHg.regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for a ceramic, enamelled or glass food-contact article in any basis. A fired inorganic matrix supplies no methyl donor.
MeHg.jurisdictions_checked: EU (Reg (EU) 1935/2004 framework + Annex I material families; Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II element list, as amended by 2016/1416 and 2020/1245); UK (retained Reg 10/2011); US (FDA food-contact substances, 21 CFR 174-190: no element migration ceiling for these elements); Codex (no food-contact-material standard); AU-NZ (FSANZ Food Standards Code 1.4.3 and 3.2.2: no element migration ceiling); Canada (Food and Drugs Act s.4 / letter-of-no-objection route, no numeric element migration ceiling); Hong Kong (Cap 132 subsidiary legislation: food limits only).
